meta.blurb: An imaginary glass lift waits on a dark rooftop. Noor says it can go as fast as she wishes, and Kit steps in. They pass the Moon, the planets and a black hole, then reach the edge of what we can see.
meta.bible: Noor: a calm, funny guide who loves the night sky. Kit: a curious young traveller who asks the questions. Skylift: an imaginary glass lift that climbs from the rooftop of an old house in a quiet town and can go as fast as Noor wishes. Tour order: Earth, the Moon, the Sun, the planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, the Asteroid belt, Pluto and the Kuiper belt, Comets, Voyager, nearby stars, Nebulae, Exoplanets, the death of stars, Neutron stars, Black holes, the Milky Way, Andromeda, deep space, the Big Bang, Dark matter and Dark energy. Real facts used: the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away; light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second; the Sun is about 150 million kilometres away and its light takes about eight minutes to reach us; the Sun and the Solar System are about four and a half billion years old; Proxima Centauri is the nearest star after the Sun, about four light-years away; the Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across; Andromeda is about two and a half million light-years away; the universe is almost fourteen billion years old. Key terms: Gravity, Fusion, Hydrogen, Helium, Galaxy, Atom, Telescope, Asteroid, Crater, Supernova, Pulsar, Spacecraft, Planet, Orbit, Nebula, Carbon, Iron, Oxygen. Voice: warm, wondering and clear; every number is real or marked "about"; no invented facts.

beats.scene: Noor and Kit stand on a dark rooftop beside a glass lift
beats.summary: Kit meets Noor on a rooftop at night, and Noor offers to show him the whole universe.

beats.scene: The lift rises and the lights of the town shrink below
beats.summary: The Skylift rises, and the town becomes a small patch of light.

beats.scene: Earth glows blue and white against black space, with a thin edge of air
beats.summary: From above, Earth looks like a blue ball with a very thin layer of air.

beats.scene: Kit looks at the grey Moon, with Earth tiny beside it
beats.summary: The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away, about thirty Earths across the gap.

beats.scene: Kit stands on grey dust beside old footprints and a crater
beats.summary: The Moon has craters and no air, and old footprints still lie in its dust.

beats.scene: The Moon hangs over a sea and the water rises on the shore
beats.summary: The Moon pulls on the oceans to make tides, and it shows Earth the same face.

beats.scene: A beam of light races past planets as Kit watches
beats.summary: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second, and nothing is faster.

beats.scene: The Sun shines huge and gold, with a thin line of Earth far away
beats.summary: The Sun is a star, and its light takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.

beats.scene: The Sun beside a line of tiny Earths, with a glowing core
beats.summary: More than a million Earths would fit inside the Sun, and its centre is extremely hot.

beats.scene: Bright gas pours out of the Sun's glowing centre
beats.summary: The Sun shines by fusion, which joins hydrogen atoms to make helium and light.

beats.scene: A small grey planet with cliffs and craters, half in sunlight
beats.summary: Mercury is small and close to the Sun, with no air to hold the heat.

beats.scene: Thick yellow clouds cover a bright planet
beats.summary: Venus is wrapped in thick clouds and is the hottest planet of all.

beats.scene: Earth shines blue with oceans, clouds and green land
beats.summary: Earth has liquid water and the right distance from the Sun, and it is the only known home of life.

beats.scene: A red desert planet with a giant mountain at the horizon
beats.summary: Mars is red from rusty dust, and its mountain Olympus Mons is among the tallest known in the Solar System.

beats.scene: A small wheeled robot stands beside dry river stones on Mars
beats.summary: Dry riverbeds on Mars show that water once flowed there, and robots search for signs of old life.

beats.scene: Rocks of many sizes float in a loose ring around the Sun
beats.summary: The asteroid belt is a wide ring of rocks between Mars and Jupiter, and Ceres is its biggest world.

beats.scene: A huge rock falls through a red sky towards the ground, long ago
beats.summary: An asteroid about ten kilometres wide hit Earth about 66 million years ago, and the dinosaurs died out.

beats.scene: A small spacecraft flies towards a tiny asteroid in dark space
beats.summary: In 2022 a spacecraft hit a small asteroid and changed its path, showing that Earth could one day be protected.

beats.scene: Jupiter fills the window with bands of cloud and a giant red storm
beats.summary: Jupiter is the biggest planet, a ball of gas with a huge storm called the Great Red Spot.

beats.scene: Four moons glow near Jupiter, one with fiery volcanoes and one icy
beats.summary: Jupiter has dozens of moons, and Io has volcanoes while Europa hides an ocean under its ice.

beats.scene: Saturn floats with wide shining rings against the black sky
beats.summary: Saturn's rings are made of ice, from tiny grains to big blocks, and they are very thin.

beats.scene: A small moon with orange air and a moon sending up icy jets
beats.summary: Titan has thick orange air and lakes of liquid gas, and Enceladus shoots water into space.

beats.scene: Two blue planets, one tipped on its side, far from the Sun
beats.summary: Uranus spins on its side and Neptune has the fastest winds, and Neptune was found by mathematics.

beats.scene: A small icy world with a pale heart-shaped plain
beats.summary: Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, and a spacecraft flew past it in 2015.

beats.scene: A comet with a long glowing tail passes near the Sun
beats.summary: A comet is a ball of ice and dust, and its tail points away from the Sun.

beats.scene: A small old spacecraft with a dish and a golden disc in dark space
beats.summary: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and is now the farthest human-made object, with a golden record.

beats.scene: A glowing line of light measured against a faint pair of stars
beats.summary: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, and the nearest star is about four of them away.

beats.scene: A grapefruit on a table with a map showing a tiny dot far away
beats.summary: If the Sun were a grapefruit, the next star would be about 3,000 kilometres away.

beats.scene: Stars of blue, white and red shine against the dark
beats.summary: Stars have different colours, and the colour shows how hot each one is.

beats.scene: A cloud of pink and blue gas glows with new stars inside
beats.summary: Stars are born inside clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, where gravity pulls the gas together.

beats.scene: A spinning disc of dust around a baby star, with small lumps forming
beats.summary: Planets form from the spinning disc around a young star, and our Solar System formed about four and a half billion years ago.

beats.scene: Telescope in space points at a distant orange star with small dark planets
beats.summary: Astronomers have found thousands of planets around other stars, called exoplanets, since 1995.

beats.scene: A far-off planet with a thin blue ring of air before its star
beats.summary: Telescopes can study the air of some exoplanets, but we do not yet know if there is life anywhere else.

beats.scene: A small red star and a huge blue star side by side
beats.summary: Small red stars live for trillions of years, but huge stars live only a few million.

beats.scene: The Sun swells into a red ball, then shrinks to a small white one
beats.summary: In about five billion years, the Sun will swell into a red giant and then fade to a white dwarf.

beats.scene: A giant star explodes in a bright flash with colourful clouds of gas
beats.summary: A very big star ends in a supernova, an explosion that for a time shines as bright as a whole galaxy.

beats.scene: Kit holds his own hand up against a sky full of stars
beats.summary: Almost every atom in your body, except hydrogen, was made inside a star.

beats.scene: A tiny dense star with a beam of light sweeping across the dark
beats.summary: A neutron star is the tiny, heavy core of a dead star, and a pulsar flashes like a lighthouse.

beats.scene: A black sphere bends the light of stars around it
beats.summary: A black hole has gravity so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.

beats.scene: A wide spiral of billions of stars seen from far above
beats.summary: The Milky Way is our galaxy, with hundreds of billions of stars, and it is about 100,000 light-years across.

beats.scene: A huge glowing core in the heart of the galaxy with stars circling it
beats.summary: At the centre of the Milky Way is a black hole about four million times the mass of the Sun.

beats.scene: A big spiral galaxy glows in the night sky above a mountain
beats.summary: The Andromeda galaxy is about two and a half million light-years away and is the farthest thing most people can see.

beats.scene: Two spiral galaxies drift together and mingle their stars
beats.summary: Andromeda and the Milky Way will probably merge in about four or five billion years.

beats.scene: A tiny dark patch of sky filled with thousands of galaxies of different shapes
beats.summary: A tiny patch of sky shows thousands of galaxies, and the whole universe holds hundreds of billions.

beats.scene: A faint red galaxy at the edge of sight beside a clock face
beats.summary: Looking far away means looking into the past, because light takes time to arrive.

beats.scene: Dots on a balloon move apart as the balloon is blown up
beats.summary: Galaxies are moving apart because space itself is expanding, as Edwin Hubble found in 1929.

beats.scene: A bright glow fills the whole dark sky and fades to stars
beats.summary: The Big Bang was the hot, dense start of the universe almost fourteen billion years ago, and its glow can still be measured.

beats.scene: Noor and Kit see a mostly dark sky with a few bright clumps
beats.summary: Ordinary matter is only about five parts in a hundred of the universe, and the rest is dark matter and dark energy.

beats.scene: A glowing sphere of the visible universe, with a dark edge beyond
beats.summary: We can only see the observable universe, and what lies beyond is unknown.

beats.scene: Kit stands on the rooftop again with Noor, the town quiet below the stars
beats.summary: Kit is back on the rooftop, a small part of the universe that can understand it.

B1B2: Kit had climbed to the rooftop to look at the stars, and there he met Noor, who smiled as if she had been waiting. She pointed to a glass lift called the Skylift and promised him a tour of the universe.
The Skylift lifted them smoothly into the dark, and the houses became a small patch of light. Every star Kit could see, Noor said, belongs to one great family of stars.
From far above, Earth looked like a blue and white ball hanging in the dark. Most of its air lies in the first ten kilometres or so, a layer as thin as the skin on an apple.
The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from Earth, a distance that would hold about thirty Earths side by side. Light takes just over a second to cross it.
The Moon has no air and no wind, so the footprints left by astronauts are still there. Twelve people walked on its dust between 1969 and 1972, and the marks may last a very long time.
The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and lifts the water twice a day to make the tides. It also turns slowly, so that it always shows us the same face.
Light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second, which is enough to circle Earth seven times in one second. As far as we know, nothing can go faster.
The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away, so its light needs about eight minutes to reach us. Noor reminded Kit that it is not a fire or a lamp but a star, like all the others.
The Sun is so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. Its centre reaches about 15 million degrees, far hotter than its golden surface.

Deep inside the Sun, the pressure is so high that hydrogen atoms join together to make helium, in a process called fusion. Each second it turns about four million tonnes of matter into light and heat.
Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no air, so its days are scorching and its nights are freezing.
Venus is wrapped in thick clouds of carbon dioxide, which trap the Sun's heat like a heavy blanket. It is hotter than Mercury, about 465 degrees on its surface.
Earth is not too hot and not too cold, so water stays liquid on its surface. It is the only place we know that has life.
Mars looks red because its dust contains a lot of iron that has rusted. Its mountain Olympus Mons is about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.
Dry riverbeds and smooth stones show that water once flowed across Mars, long ago. Robots with wheels now drive there, looking for signs that tiny life may once have existed.
Between Mars and Jupiter lies a wide ring of rocks called the Asteroid belt. Do not worry, Noor said, because the rocks are very far apart.
Space rocks sometimes hit our planet, and the Moon's craters show how often it has happened. About 66 million years ago, one about ten kilometres wide struck, and most dinosaurs died.
In 2022 a spacecraft called DART flew into a small asteroid on purpose. It changed the path of the rock, which was a test to protect Earth.
Jupiter is the biggest planet, so big that more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside. It has no solid ground, only gas, and a great storm that has been seen for at least 150 years.
Jupiter has dozens of moons, and each one is a world of its own. Io is covered in volcanoes, and Europa has a shell of ice with a deep ocean of salty water below.
Saturn is famous for its bright rings, which are made of billions of pieces of ice. They are very wide, but they are extremely thin.
Saturn's moon Titan has thick orange air and lakes of liquid methane. Another moon, Enceladus, shoots jets of water into space.
Uranus and Neptune are cold, blue worlds far from the Sun. Uranus spins on its side, and Neptune has some of the fastest winds in the Solar System.
Pluto is a small, icy world that scientists now call a dwarf planet. In 2015 a spacecraft flew past it and sent home pictures.
A comet is a ball of ice and dust. When it comes near the Sun, it heats up and grows a long tail that points away from it.
The spacecraft Voyager 1 left Earth in 1977 and is still travelling today. It is now the farthest human-made object, and it carries a golden record of sounds from Earth.
A light-year is the distance that light travels in one year, almost ten trillion kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is just over four light-years away.
Noor said to shrink the Sun to the size of a grapefruit. On that scale, the nearest star would be about 3,000 kilometres away.
Look closely and you will see that stars have different colours. Blue stars are the hottest, and red stars are cooler.
Stars are born in huge clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. Gravity pulls the gas together, and in the end a new star lights up.
Around a young star, a spinning disc of dust and gas remains. Dust sticks together, grows into rocks, and in time becomes planets.
Until 1995 nobody had found a planet around a star like the Sun. Since then, astronomers have found thousands of these planets, called exoplanets.
New telescopes can now study the air of some of these distant planets by looking at starlight. Nobody knows yet whether life exists anywhere else, but many people hope to find out.
Not all stars live for the same length of time. The small ones burn slowly and live for trillions of years, but big ones burn fast and die young.
The Sun is about halfway through its life, and it has about five billion years left. After that it will swell up, then shrink to a small, faint, white star.
When a very big star runs out of fuel, it collapses and then explodes as a supernova. For a short time it shines as bright as a whole galaxy.
The carbon in your body and the iron in your blood were made inside stars. When those stars exploded, they spread these atoms through space.
A neutron star is the small core left after a big star dies. It is only about twenty kilometres wide, but a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes.
When a very big star collapses, it can form a black hole. Its gravity is so strong that even light cannot escape from it.
Our home is the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across. It contains hundreds of billions of stars, and the Sun is only one of them.
At the centre of the Milky Way lives a giant black hole. Astronomers watched the stars near it move, and in 2022 they took its picture.
On a dark night, the Andromeda galaxy appears as a faint smudge. Its light is about two and a half million years old.
Andromeda is slowly moving towards the Milky Way, and the two galaxies are falling together. In about four or five billion years, they will probably join into one.
The Hubble telescope looked at a tiny, empty-looking patch of sky for many days. In that small patch, it found thousands of galaxies of every shape.
Light needs time to travel, so far away things look as they were long ago. A telescope is therefore a kind of time machine, and it shows us the early universe.
In the 1920s, astronomers found that far galaxies are moving away from us. The farther they are, the faster they go, so space itself is growing.
If the universe is growing, then long ago it was smaller and much hotter. That beginning was almost fourteen billion years ago, and we call it the Big Bang.
Everything we can see, from planets to galaxies, makes up only about five percent of the universe. The rest is called dark matter and dark energy, and nobody knows what they are.
We can only see as far as light has had time to reach us. Beyond that edge, the universe may go on, but we do not know.
The Skylift settled on the roof, and Kit stood again beneath the same stars. He felt small, but also lucky, because he was a part of the universe that can wonder about it.
C1C2: On a cold, clear night, a boy named Kit climbed onto the roof of an old house to look at the stars, and found a woman named Noor already sitting there with a flask of tea. She nodded towards a glass lift that had not been there the day before, and explained that it could carry them anywhere he liked. If he was willing to come, she said, she would show him everything there is, as far as anyone has ever seen.

Without a sound, the Skylift slid upwards, and the streets and houses below melted into a small, glowing patch. Noor told him that every single star he could see with his own eyes belongs to one enormous family of stars, which astronomers call a galaxy. That family, she added with a smile, was only the beginning of the story.

Seen from this height, the planet seemed to hang in the blackness like a blue and white marble, wrapped in a faint, glowing edge of air. Almost all of that air lies in the lowest ten kilometres or so, Noor said. This makes the protective layer around us astonishingly thin compared with the size of the world.

Their first stop was the Moon, which hangs about 384,000 kilometres from Earth, far enough that you could line up about thirty Earths in the gap between them. Light, the fastest traveller in the universe, covers that whole distance in little more than a second. A car on a motorway, by contrast, would need months of steady driving day and night to get there.

On the grey, silent surface, Kit saw craters everywhere, the scars of rocks that had struck the Moon billions of years ago. Because there is no wind or rain to wear anything away, footprints can survive in the dust for an extraordinarily long time. Twelve astronauts walked here between 1969 and 1972, and their tracks are still waiting for the next visitors.

Noor explained that the Moon's gravity tugs on the oceans of Earth, raising and lowering the water twice a day in the rhythm we call the tides. The Moon also spins at exactly the pace of its orbit, so it always turns the same face towards us. For that reason, nobody on Earth has ever seen its far side without help from a spacecraft.

Noor taught Kit the most important number of the tour, the speed of light, which is about 300,000 kilometres every second. At that speed a beam could race around Earth seven times before you had finished a single blink. As far as anyone has ever been able to show, nothing in the universe can overtake it.

Next they approached the Sun, which lies about 150 million kilometres from Earth, so far that its light takes about eight minutes to arrive. Noor told Kit that the Sun is not a lamp or a bonfire but an ordinary star, and that it only looks special because we live so close. Every other star in the sky, she said, is a sun that happens to be very far away.

Noor held up her hands to show how vast the Sun is, so vast that more than a million Earths could be packed inside it. Deep in its centre the temperature reaches about 15 million degrees, far hotter than the golden surface that we see. That fierce heat, she said, is what keeps the whole star alive and shining for billions of years.

The Sun shines because, in its crushing centre, atoms of hydrogen are forced together to form helium, a process known as fusion. Every second it turns about four million tonnes of matter into pure energy, and it escapes as heat and light. Astonishingly, it has been doing this without a pause for about four and a half billion years.

The first planet outward from the Sun is Mercury, a small, grey world of cliffs and craters that circles very close to the blaze. With almost no air to hold the heat, its sunlit side becomes hot enough to melt lead. On the night side, however, the temperature drops to a bitter, lifeless cold that no living thing could bear.

Venus, wrapped in thick clouds of carbon dioxide, is the hottest planet of all, with a surface temperature of about 465 degrees. The gas traps the Sun's heat like a heavy blanket, which is why it is hotter even than Mercury. It also turns so slowly that one of its days lasts longer than its year.

The third planet is Earth, which sits at just the right distance from the Sun for water to stay liquid in its oceans and rivers. So far it is the only place in the universe where we know for certain that life exists. Noor asked Kit to remember that fact as they travelled on, because it makes our home precious.

Mars is a cold, dry desert, and its colour comes from rusty iron in the dust that covers the ground. Rising above the plains is Olympus Mons, a volcano about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest. It is among the tallest mountains that anyone has found in the whole Solar System.

The rocks of Mars tell a story of rivers and lakes that dried up billions of years ago, and wheeled robots called rovers now study them. Dry channels and smooth, rounded stones show that water once flowed across the land. The rovers are searching for any trace of ancient life, but so far none has been found, and the question is still open.

Between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, Noor steered the Skylift through the asteroid belt, a wide ring of rocky leftovers from the birth of the planets. In films these rocks crowd together and crash against one another in a dangerous storm of stone. In truth they are so far apart that a spacecraft can cross the belt almost without meeting one.

Noor reminded Kit that space rocks do sometimes strike our planet, and she showed him a picture of a huge crater. About 66 million years ago, an asteroid roughly ten kilometres wide hit the Earth with terrible force. Most scientists agree that this event helped to end the age of the dinosaurs.

Today astronomers watch the sky for dangerous rocks, and in 2022 a spacecraft named DART crashed on purpose into a small asteroid. The experiment slightly changed the rock's orbit, which proved for the first time that humans can push an asteroid off its path. If one is ever headed our way, we may now have a plan to protect our home.

Jupiter is the giant of the Solar System, large enough to hold more than 1,300 Earths, and it is made almost entirely of gas, with no ground to land on. Across its stripes of cloud sits the Great Red Spot, a storm wider than our planet. Astronomers have watched it for at least 150 years, and it is still turning today.

Jupiter has dozens of moons, and Noor said that each of them is a world of its own. Io is covered in erupting volcanoes, while Europa hides a vast ocean of salty water beneath its shell of ice. That hidden ocean makes Europa one of the best places to look for life beyond Earth.

The rings of Saturn look like solid sheets, but they are actually billions of pieces of ice, some as small as grains of sand and some as large as houses. Although they stretch for hundreds of thousands of kilometres from side to side, they are astonishingly thin. Compared with their width, even a sheet of paper would seem thick, and that is what makes the rings so delicate.

Among the moons of Saturn, Titan stands out for its thick orange air and its rivers and lakes of liquid methane. Tiny Enceladus is just as strange, because it throws jets of water from cracks in its ice. These jets seem to come from a salty ocean hidden far below the surface, and scientists find that exciting.

Uranus and Neptune are the two most distant planets, cold blue giants of ice and gas, and Uranus spins tipped over on its side. Neptune is wild with winds that rank among the fastest in the Solar System. In 1846, astronomers found it by calculation first, because the strange wandering of Uranus told them that another large planet must be pulling on it.

Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper belt, a wide region of icy bodies, and its most famous member is Pluto, which was renamed a dwarf planet in 2006. Many people still argue about whether the new name is fair, and Noor said that Pluto does not seem to mind. When the spacecraft New Horizons flew past in 2015, it revealed mountains of ice and a smooth, heart-shaped plain.

Comets are balls of ice and dust, sometimes called dirty snowballs, that spend most of their lives in the freezing dark. As one nears the Sun, the heat releases gas and dust, and a glowing tail stretches out behind it. The tail always points away from the Sun, whichever way the comet happens to be moving.

In 1977 Voyager 1 began a journey that has never stopped, and in 2012 it became the first human-made thing to enter the space between the stars. It carries a golden record of music, greetings and sounds from Earth, in case anyone ever finds it. Its radio signals, travelling at the speed of light, now need nearly a day to reach us.

Kilometres are too small for the space between the stars, so astronomers use the light-year, the distance that light travels in a year, almost ten trillion kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, lies just over four light-years away. Voyager, at its present speed, would need more than 70,000 years to reach it, which is far longer than all of written history.

To show how empty space is, Noor asked Kit to imagine the Sun shrunk to the size of a grapefruit. On that scale the Earth would be a grain of sand, a few metres away. The nearest star would be another grapefruit about 3,000 kilometres away, with almost nothing in between.

If you look carefully at the night sky, you will notice that the stars are not all white, but shine in shades of blue, white, yellow and red. The colour is a kind of thermometer, Noor said, because it tells us how hot the surface of each star is. Blue stars are the hottest of all, red stars are the coolest, and our yellow Sun sits somewhere in between.

Noor took Kit to the Orion Nebula, a glowing cloud that can be seen as a faint smudge with the naked eye on a clear winter night. Inside such a cloud, gravity slowly pulls the gas and dust into dense clumps over a very long time. When one clump grows hot enough in its centre, a new star switches on.

Around every new star there is a spinning disc of leftover gas and dust, and in it, tiny grains stick together and slowly grow into rocks. Over millions of years, the rocks collide and merge until the largest of them become planets. Our own Solar System was formed in just this way about four and a half billion years ago.

In 1995 astronomers found the first planet orbiting a star like our Sun, and since then they have discovered thousands more, called exoplanets. They come in every kind, from hot giants that whirl around their stars in a few days to small, rocky worlds. Some of the rocky ones might, perhaps, have oceans of liquid water on their surfaces.

The newest space telescopes can detect which gases are in the air of a few of these worlds, by studying starlight that passes through it. Noor was honest with Kit that nobody yet knows whether life exists anywhere else. She thought that finding out might be one of the greatest discoveries ever made.

Surprisingly, the biggest stars live the shortest lives, because they burn their fuel so wildly that they last only a few million years. Small red stars, by contrast, sip theirs so slowly that they may shine for trillions of years. That is far longer than the universe itself has existed so far, which means that none of them has yet died of old age.

The Sun is about halfway through its life, and in roughly five billion years it will run short of hydrogen. It will then swell into a red giant, puffing off its outer layers like a smoke ring. What remains will shrink into a white dwarf, a glowing ember about the size of Earth.

Stars far bigger than the Sun end their lives in a spectacular blast that can be seen across great distances. When the fuel runs out, the core collapses in a moment, and the explosion that follows is called a supernova. For a few weeks it can shine as brightly as an entire galaxy of stars.

Noor told Kit something that made him look at his own hands in the starlight. Apart from hydrogen, which dates from the beginning of the universe, nearly every atom in his body was made inside a star. The carbon in his cells and the iron in his blood were scattered through space by stars that exploded long ago.

Sometimes the core left behind by a supernova becomes a neutron star, an object only about twenty kilometres across, yet heavier than the Sun. A single teaspoon of its matter would weigh billions of tonnes, more than a mountain. Some neutron stars spin many times a second and sweep a beam of radio waves across space like a lighthouse, and we call these pulsars.

The heaviest stars can collapse into black holes, regions where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. Noor laughed that they are not cosmic vacuum cleaners, and that they only pull on things that come very close. If the Sun became one, Earth would simply carry on orbiting as before, though in the dark.

The Skylift climbed high above the Milky Way and revealed its spiral shape, about 100,000 light-years from edge to edge. The Sun is just one of its hundreds of billions of stars, sitting about 26,000 light-years from the centre in a quiet part of the spiral. It takes about 230 million years to go around the galaxy once, and it has only done so about twenty times.

At the heart of the galaxy hides a black hole about four million times as heavy as the Sun. Astronomers worked out its size by watching the stars that whirl around it at enormous speed. In 2022 they finally published a picture of the glowing gas around it, which is the closest anyone can come to seeing it.

Away from city lights, the Andromeda galaxy can be seen with the naked eye as a faint, pale smudge, and it is the most distant thing most people will ever see. Its light began its journey about two and a half million years ago, long before our own species existed. Our earliest ancestors were then only just learning to make simple tools from stone and bone.

Andromeda is slowly falling towards the Milky Way, and astronomers think the two galaxies will merge in about four or five billion years. Stars are so far apart that very few of them will actually collide when the great clouds of stars pass through each other. The meeting will be less a crash than a slow, glittering dance that lasts for millions of years.

Astronomers once pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a patch of sky so small that it looked empty, and left it there for days. The picture showed about ten thousand galaxies, each one a vast city of stars, in a space no bigger than a grain of sand held at arm's length. This suggests that the whole observable universe contains hundreds of billions of galaxies in all.

Because light needs time to travel, a telescope is also a kind of time machine, and every distant view is really a view of the past. The faintest galaxies seen by the newest space telescope are shown as they were more than thirteen billion years ago. At that time, the universe was still very young and the first stars were only just beginning to shine.

By the late 1920s, Edwin Hubble and others had found that nearly all distant galaxies are rushing away from us, and the farther away they are, the faster they go. It is not that the galaxies are flying through space, but that space itself is stretching. Imagine dots drawn on a balloon that is being blown up, and you will see how the dots move apart.

Run the expansion backwards, and everything was once packed into a state of enormous heat and density, almost fourteen billion years ago. This was not an explosion in space, like a firework, but rather the growth of space itself. Its faint afterglow, discovered in 1965, still reaches us from every direction, and it can be measured with careful instruments.

Here Noor grew serious, because the planets, stars and galaxies we can see make up only about five percent of the universe. About a quarter is dark matter, which pulls on galaxies but gives out no light. The remainder is dark energy, which seems to push space apart faster and faster, and nobody yet knows what either one really is.

The part of the universe that we can see is limited by how far light has travelled since the Big Bang, and we call it the observable universe. Noor said that beyond it there may be much more, perhaps even an endless amount of space and stars. At present, however, nobody can see it or say for sure, and that honest uncertainty is part of the adventure.

When the Skylift touched down on the rooftop, the town was still asleep and the same stars shone overhead, but Kit saw them differently. Noor told him that he was a small part of the universe, and that he should never be ashamed of being small. He was also the part that had learned to look back at it, to measure it, and to ask questions.
